rationale: All 6 candidates are direct matches (trait_reported/trait_efo and phenotyping_reported all indicate abdominal aortic aneurysm), so selection hinges on endpoint fidelity plus PRS-comparable performance evidence and study archetype. PGS000753 is preferred because it is disease-focused (AAA architecture in MVP/MAYO-VDB) and provides the clearest PRS-specific discriminative signal via an effect size (OR per SD 1.37, 95% CI 1.30–1.44) with basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), whereas most others report only full-model AUROC/C-index or weakly comparable metrics. Runners-up are the two Nat Genet meta-analysis PRS-CS scores (PGS003972/PGS003973) because they come from a large, disease-focused multi-cohort AAA GWAS meta-analysis with direct AAA phenotyping; however, their reported discrimination is only full-model AUROC/C-index (0.69 and 0.882) without explicit PRS-only metrics, making cross-model comparison uncertain (and the very high C-index is likely covariate-driven given covariates include age/sex). Overall confidence is moderate because no candidate provides a clearly comparable PRS-only AUROC, and several candidates are from framework/portability-style papers (PGS001784, PGS002054) where reported metrics (e.g., partial-r ~0.0144; R2 ~0.0147) are hard to compare directly against effect-size-only reporting. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All four candidates are direct matches to the target concept (alcohol dependence) via trait_efo/phenotyping_reported alignment: PGS002738/PGS002739 are explicitly mapped to trait_efo="alcohol dependence" with phenotyping_reported="Alcohol use disorder"; PGS000201/PGS000202 are mapped to "alcohol dependence measurement" but still use DSM-5 alcohol use disorder criteria counts (close endpoint fidelity). PGS002738 is best supported because it is the most endpoint-faithful (trait_efo exactly alcohol dependence; phenotyping is AUD diagnosis) and provides the strongest visible discriminative evidence among the EUR-evaluated options (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.96, 95% CI 1.54–2.51) with a reasonably large EUR validation sample (n=7,900). Runners-up: PGS000201 and PGS000202 are near-clone direct matches from the same publication with the same AUD DSM-5 criteria endpoint; among them PGS000201 has stronger incremental ΔR² vs covariates (0.01192 vs 0.00456) and a larger validation sample (n=7,599 vs 1,251), so it ranks above PGS000202. Main limitation lowering confidence: no candidate reports clearly PRS-only AUROC/R², covariates are unknown for PGS002738 (comparability uncertainty), and PGS002739 is strong but evaluated only in African American/Afro-Caribbean samples (making it less generally supported without a specified target ancestry), so the best choice is supported but not unequivocal.

All three candidates are direct matches to the target trait (trait_efo = alcoholic liver cirrhosis) with endpoint-faithful phenotyping labels. PGS004913 is best supported because it is explicitly disease-focused on alcohol-associated cirrhosis among heavy drinkers, uses basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), and reports PRS-comparable signal (R²=0.029) plus a meaningful risk gradient (OR top vs bottom deciles 4.4). The main limitation is that its reported metric is R² (not PRS-only AUROC) and the training/validation sample sizes are modest, so cross-study comparability remains limited.

Runner-up PGS001777 is also disease-focused and reports strong stratification (OR top 20% vs bottom 20% = 6.18) with an AUROC=0.671, but the AUROC appears to be a full-model metric (not explicitly PGS-only), covariates are unknown, validation is small (n=1,390), and phenotyping_reported is restricted to males, reducing generality.

Second runner-up PGS000704 has clean/basic covariates and very large UKB training/validation with a C-index=0.711, but it comes from a broad biomarker genetics paper (more framework-like context) and only full-model time-to-event discrimination is shown (no PRS-only AUC/R²), with a modest per-SD HR=1.18—so its PRS-specific contribution is unclear despite the large sample size.

All 19 candidates are direct matches to angina pectoris (trait_efo=angina pectoris; phenotyping_reported variants include ICD10 I20 and PheCode 411.3). Among models with PRS-comparable metrics, the UKB snpnet family (PGS001260/PGS001261/PGS001262) reports explicit PGS-only AUROC (~0.58) and PGS-only R² (~0.012–0.013), which are interpretable and below the provided local heritability ceiling (h2_obs ~0.009–0.014; liability h2 ~0.134), supporting metric plausibility. PGS001261 is preferred because it is explicitly angina pectoris (time-to-event) with the strongest reported full-model discrimination in this snpnet cluster (full-model AUROC 0.7485) while retaining similar PGS-only metrics and basic covariates (age/sex/array/PCs), making it the most consistently supported within the best-documented direct-match cluster. Runners-up: PGS001260 is nearly identical evidence-wise (same study, similar PGS-only metrics) but slightly weaker full-model AUROC; PGS001262 has the highest full-model AUROC (0.8073) and slightly higher PGS-only AUROC/R², but its endpoint is a more specific self/doctor-reported phrasing (“Vascular/heart problems diagnosed by doctor Angina”), which introduces some endpoint heterogeneity versus the generic target. Confidence is not High because several newer ICD10/PheCode models (e.g., PGS004457/PGS004527 and PGS005048/PGS005052/PGS005057) report only full-model C-index or per-SD OR without clear PRS-only AUROC/R², making cross-family ranking uncertain; additionally, the snpnet models come from a pan-trait UKB framework paper, which domain guidance flags as potentially less externally robust despite clean metadata. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All 9 candidates are direct matches to ankylosing spondylitis by trait_efo, and most also by phenotyping_reported. The strongest comparable PRS evidence in the visible set comes from the UKB snpnet models (PGS001267/PGS001268), which uniquely report PRS-comparable metrics including PGS-only AUROC and PGS R² (no covariates) plus incremental AUROC with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array). Between these siblings, PGS001267 is the cleaner generic case-control endpoint (phenotyping_reported: ankylosing spondylitis) versus PGS001268 being explicitly time-to-event (TTE), which domain guidance flags as a mild endpoint penalty for a generic disease target despite slightly higher full-model AUROC/R². As runners-up, PGS001268 remains strongly supported due to similar endpoint alignment and similarly rich PRS-only metrics, while among the remaining models PGS002089 is preferred because it has the strongest available PRS-comparable metric in that subgroup (partial correlation 0.0919) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method with many variants, whereas the Taiwanese EAS-only models report only full-model AUROC with unknown covariates (not PRS-comparable) and the other portability sibling (PGS001876) has a weaker partial correlation (0.0797). Overall confidence is moderated because the best-supported models come from a pan-trait UKB framework paper (a known generalization risk per domain knowledge), and several alternatives lack PRS-only metrics, limiting cross-study comparability.

Direct-match candidates for the target trait (aortic stenosis) are present: PGS005252, PGS005254, PGS005255, and PGS005256 (others are hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and are not direct matches). PGS005252 is best supported because it is an exact trait/EFO match with endpoint-fidelity phenotyping (“Incident aortic stenosis cases”), uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDPred2) with a large variant set (1,119,377), and reports a strong time-to-event effect size (HR=1.92) plus a high full-model C-index (0.87) in a very large evaluation sample (n=446,895). The main limitation is that the reported discrimination is a full-model metric with substantial clinical covariates (multiple cardiometabolic comorbidities and exposures), and no PRS-only AUROC/R² is provided, so the PRS-specific contribution cannot be cleanly compared across candidates.

Runners-up: PGS005254 is also an exact aortic stenosis model with incident endpoint and a moderate-to-strong HR (1.64, with CI), but lacks comparable discrimination metrics and has smaller evaluation (n=244,450). Between the remaining two, PGS005255 and PGS005256 are aortic-valve-function measurement-labeled scores but still use incident aortic stenosis phenotyping; they have similar HRs (~1.53) and identical evaluation size/covariates, so they are effectively tied—PGS005255 is selected as the second runner-up arbitrarily only insofar as it is equally supported by the visible evidence. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

Direct-match candidates for the target trait (arthritis) are present, including an exact-label model (PGS001135; trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all "Arthritis (nos)"/"arthritis") and two additional arthritis-labeled models (PGS004477 and PGS004547; both "M13 (Other arthritis)" with trait_efo="arthritis"). PGS001135 is best supported on endpoint fidelity because it is explicitly the generic arthritis phenotype (not a specific subtype like RA, OA, gout, etc.) and provides PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.53928; PGS R2=0.00291) plus incremental AUROC (0.00314), enabling interpretation beyond full-model AUROC. The main limitation is that PGS001135 comes from a pan-trait UK Biobank framework study ("Significant sparse polygenic risk scores across 813 traits"), which domain guidance flags as often underperforming disease-focused models; however, within the visible candidate list there is no clearly disease-focused, generic-arthritis (non-subtype) alternative with stronger, PRS-comparable performance evidence. The runners-up are PGS004477 and PGS004547 because they are also mapped to arthritis (trait_efo="arthritis"), but they have weaker visible evidence: no AUC/R2 and only modest ORs (~1.20 and ~1.26) with unknown covariates, making them less directly comparable and less informative than PGS001135.

All listed candidates are direct matches to asthma (trait_efo=asthma), but they vary in endpoint fidelity and PRS-comparable evidence. PGS002727 is best supported overall because it is explicitly disease-focused for asthma ("Multiancestral polygenic risk score for pediatric asthma"), uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS; 985,837 variants), reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.57, 95% CI 1.55–1.60) and provides a large validation sample (n=391,820) with AUROC=0.66 (noting this is a full-model metric and covariates are listed as Unknown, which lowers comparability confidence). Runner-up PGS001344 has strong PRS-comparable metrics reported (PGS-only AUROC=0.64568; PGS-only R2=0.05973; incremental AUROC=0.07977) and a clear endpoint (doctor-diagnosed asthma), but it comes from a pan-trait UK Biobank framework paper ("across 813 traits"), which domain guidance flags as typically less reliable in external validation than disease-focused models. Second runner-up PGS001782 is a genome-wide PRS-CS-auto score from a broad multi-biobank study (Cell Genom) with supportive PRS-comparable R2 (Nagelkerke R2 with covariates regressed out = 0.048844) and AUROC=0.659, but it is more framework/benchmarking-oriented and has less endpoint-specific framing than PGS002727. Main limitation: the top choice (PGS002727) is pediatric-asthma-specific (endpoint mismatch risk for generic asthma) and has unknown covariates with only full-model AUROC reported, so while it is the most coherent disease-focused evidence package in the visible list, the selection is not high-confidence.

All 6 candidates are direct matches at the EFO level (atopic eczema), but endpoint fidelity differs materially. PGS002755 is the best-supported for generic atopic eczema risk because its phenotyping is directly aligned to the target (“Incident atopic dermatitis”), it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS; 1,090,702 variants), and it reports a PRS-associated effect size in a very large European evaluation sample (HR high vs low PRS 1.249, n=337,910). Runner-up PGS004587 has similarly aligned incident atopic dermatitis phenotyping and a large European evaluation sample with an HR (1.153), but it is a sparse genome-wide-significant SNP score (23 variants), which is structurally less favorable for a polygenic trait than PRS-CS. Runner-up PGS001773 is endpoint-aligned to atopic eczema but restricted to “Moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis” and uses only 25 variants; its very high reported full-model AUROC (0.93) is discounted because it is not PGS-only and includes multiple non-genetic covariates (age/sex/parental ethnicity), making PRS contribution unclear. Overall confidence is moderate (not high) because none of the candidates report clearly PRS-only AUROC/R², several are therapy-specific paradoxical eczema endpoints in psoriasis patients (PGS003459/PGS003486/PGS004903) which are weaker matches for generic atopic eczema, and the top choice relies on HR rather than directly comparable PRS-only discrimination metrics.

All shortlisted models are direct matches to atrial fibrillation by trait_reported/trait_efo and generally endpoint-faithful phenotyping_reported (AF diagnosis/incident AF), so ranking is driven by the strongest mutually consistent evidence package (endpoint fidelity + PRS-relevant performance/effect size + study archetype/covariates). PGS005168 is best supported because it comes from a disease-focused large AF meta-analysis (Nat Genet; many contributing cohorts listed), uses a modern genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS), and reports strong discrimination in the selected European validation record (C-index 0.8718 with CI) plus a strong per-SD effect size (HR 1.6663), with covariates that include basic demographics/array/CHARGE-AF (noted as a potential packaging concern but less severe here than explicit fixed-horizon risk wrappers). Runner-up PGS005313 is also disease-focused and multi-cohort with strong reported OR (1.82) and AUROC 0.78, but it is evaluated in a non-EUR setting (MAE 100%) and uses PRS-CSx with less directly comparable evaluation context to the EUR-centric target evidence. Second runner-up PGS002814 has very strong training scale and good reported AUROC (0.74) and pseudo-R2 (0.14) but is explicitly East-Asian evaluated (EAS 100%), making it less directly supported for general AF risk without a specified deployment ancestry. Confidence is Moderate because many candidates report only full-model metrics (often not PRS-only), covariate sets vary (including risk-calculator inclusion in some models), and several newer models show high full-model discrimination without clear PRS-only metrics, limiting clean cross-model comparability. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

Direct-match candidates are present (4 total). PGS001263 is the strongest direct match on endpoint fidelity: trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported are all specifically “Atrial flutter,” whereas the other three candidates are composite “atrial fibrillation and flutter” endpoints (one time-to-event). PGS001263 also reports PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.617 and PGS R2 0.025), enabling comparison and passing the heritability sanity-check (PGS R2 well below the provided h2 ceiling). Main limitation: it comes from a pan-trait sparse UKB framework paper (“across 813 traits”), which domain guidance flags as tending to generalize less well externally; additionally, its reported high full-model AUROC is likely covariate-influenced and should not be treated as PRS-only evidence.

Runners-up: PGS001339 is next-best because it includes atrial flutter in the endpoint and also reports PRS-only metrics, but it is a time-to-event composite phenotype (lower endpoint fidelity for a generic atrial flutter target). Between the remaining portability-study composites (PGS001841 vs PGS002050), both lack PRS-only AUROC/R2 and are otherwise very similar; PGS002050 is preferred as runner-up due to a method/structure signal (LDpred2 genome-wide shrinkage with far higher variant count) and slightly higher reported partial-r, though the evidence is limited and not directly comparable to AUROC.

Two direct-match candidates are present (both map to autism spectrum disorder). PGS000327 is best supported because its endpoint fidelity is coherent across fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all explicitly “Autism spectrum disorder”), it comes from an ASD-focused GWAS publication, and it provides supportive PRS-relevant evidence including an OR per SD of 1.33 (moderate) plus an R² metric (0.0245) in European validation with basic covariates (genetic PCs, genotyping wave). PGS002790 is a weaker runner-up because its phenotyping_reported is “Psychiatric behavior (withdrawn)”, which is an explicit endpoint mismatch/ambiguity relative to ASD despite the trait_reported label, and its reported partial R² (0.00546) is smaller; additionally, training sample size is N/A and the study framing is broader (sex-specific cross-psychiatric associations) rather than ASD-endpoint-focused. Overall confidence is Moderate (not High) because neither model reports clearly PRS-only discrimination metrics (e.g., PGS-only AUROC/R²), and the available R² values appear to be full/partial-model style metrics, limiting strict comparability.

All 20 visible candidates are direct matches to basal cell carcinoma by trait_reported/trait_efo, but they differ in endpoint fidelity and strength of reported validation evidence. PGS000452 is best supported because it has an exact BCC endpoint (phenotyping_reported: Basal cell carcinoma), basic covariates (age/sex/batch/PCs), European evaluation, and the strongest reported discrimination/effect evidence among the comparable endpoint-faithful set (full-model AUROC 0.632 with Nagelkerke R² 0.0487; OR per SD 1.663; top 1% vs rest OR 3.61). The two closest runners-up are PGS000454 (nearly identical endpoint/covariates/ancestry with essentially the same AUROC 0.632 and slightly higher top-1% OR 3.79; very similar per-SD OR 1.661) and PGS000456 (same endpoint/covariates/ancestry with AUROC 0.63, R² 0.0456, and top-1% OR 3.95). Confidence is Moderate rather than High because most candidates report only full-model AUROC (no PGS-only AUROC/R²), several near-clone models have very similar metrics, and some newer multi-cohort models (e.g., PGS003416/PGS003417) lack comparable discrimination metrics despite strong per-SD ORs, making the ranking dependent on limited, not fully PRS-isolated, performance reporting. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All three visible candidates are direct matches to the target concept via trait_efo including “bilirubin metabolism disease.” The strongest endpoint-fidelity match is the pair PGS001824/PGS002032, both explicitly targeting “Disorders of bilirubin excretion” with matching phenotyping_reported and identical reported partial-r (0.0716) in European validation; between these near-clones, PGS002032 has a stronger structural profile (LDpred2 with 19,768 variants vs 22 variants for penalized regression), so it is the best runner-up. PGS001824 is selected as best_model_id because it has the same direct endpoint alignment and comparable reported metric evidence as PGS002032, and the visible evidence does not include PRS-only AUROC/R² or effect sizes to decisively favor one sibling over the other; thus the choice remains somewhat uncertain. PGS000924 is also a direct match but is penalized for being a pan-trait UKB sparse framework score (“across 813 traits”) with a very small variant set (5) and a time-to-event composite phenotype (“porphyrin and bilirubin metabolism”), making it less endpoint-faithful and less likely to generalize despite reporting high AUROC/R²-like fields. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All three candidates are direct lexical/EFO matches to the target bipolar spectrum (PGS002786: bipolar disorder; PGS002787: bipolar I; PGS002788: bipolar II) and share the same publication, method (SDPR), EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, and similar variant counts (~935k–949k), so they form a near-clone family with limited differentiating evidence. Endpoint fidelity is a major limitation: each model’s phenotyping_reported is a non-diagnosis behavioral/cognitive phenotype (pattern comparison; Dsm5 depression; sluggish cognitive tempo) rather than bipolar disorder case/control status, which weakens direct-match support per the provided domain guidance (phenotyping_reported is primary). With no PRS-comparable AUC and only small partial R² values reported (all ~0.0025–0.0031) in modest validation samples (~2.2k–2.5k), performance evidence is weak and not clearly tied to bipolar diagnosis. PGS002786 is selected as best only because it is the only candidate whose trait_reported/trait_efo exactly matches ‘bipolar disorder’ (umbrella target) while the others are subtype-specific; however, this is only a marginal advantage given the endpoint mismatch and otherwise indistinguishable metadata. Runners-up are ordered next by remaining direct-match support: bipolar I then bipolar II.

All three candidates are direct matches at the catalog mapping level for the target concept (blood coagulation disease), but the evidence is not strong enough to yield a high-confidence winner. PGS002034 and PGS001826 are the most phenotype-specific to coagulation disease (both: "Congenital deficiency of other clotting factors (including factor VII)"; phenotyping matches the reported trait), and they come from the same UKB portability publication with very similar reported partial-r (~0.0563 vs ~0.0562) and identical training cohort/covariates/validation ancestry context, making them near-indistinguishable on endpoint and performance evidence. Between these two, PGS002034 is weakly preferred on structural grounds (LDpred2 genome-wide shrinkage with 32,552 variants vs penalized regression with 45 variants) given the domain guidance that method family/variant coverage can be used as a fallback when comparable PRS-only AUC/R2 are absent. PGS001033 is a broader/less specific endpoint ("Other coagulation defects" time-to-event) and is from a pan-trait sparse UKB framework paper (snpnet) with an extremely low variant count (1), which is a warning sign despite having explicit AUROC fields; thus it ranks behind the two congenital-deficiency models. Main limitation: none of the candidates provides clearly comparable PRS-only discrimination metrics across the set (two have only partial-r; one is a framework TTE model), so confidence remains low and the outcome is sub-optimal. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

Direct-match candidates are present (multiple models with trait_efo=breast carcinoma / phenotyping_reported=Breast cancer). Among the visible list, PGS004153 is best supported because it is endpoint-faithful (phenotyping_reported: Breast cancer), uses a multi-score aggregation method (UKBB-EUR.MultiPRS.CV; domain knowledge notes ensembles/multi-score aggregation are structurally advantaged), and has strong reported discrimination in the selected validation record (full_model_auc≈0.6625) with no added covariates (covariates=0), reducing concern that performance is covariate-driven. The two strongest runners-up from the same visible list are PGS004040 and PGS004025: both are also endpoint-faithful, covariates=0, and show very similar AUROC/R2 in the same publication family (LDpred2.CV and LDpred2-auto, respectively; full_model_auc≈0.6598). Confidence is Moderate (not High) because many breast-cancer direct matches exist in the visible list with heterogeneous endpoints/covariates, and the comparison relies heavily on full-model AUROC/R2 from one study family without broadly comparable PRS-only metrics across all candidates.

All 10 visible candidates are direct matches to celiac disease via trait_efo and largely consistent phenotyping_reported. PGS000316 is best supported because it targets an unqualified coeliac disease endpoint (high endpoint fidelity), reports strong discrimination (full-model AUROC=0.879 with tight CI) and is from a disease-focused clinical-care diagnostic study context rather than a pan-trait/portability framework; its very large validation sample size is supportive (though a weak tie-breaker per domain guidance). Key limitation: only full-model AUROC is provided (no explicit PGS-only AUROC/R²), and covariates are listed as Unknown, so the degree of covariate contribution to AUROC cannot be assessed.

Runners-up: PGS000040 is a disease-focused celiac prediction model with very high reported AUROC=0.90, but it is also full-model only with Unknown covariates and smaller validation, making comparability uncertain. PGS001301 provides explicit PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.8287; PGS R²=0.1422) with standard covariates, but it comes from a pan-trait UK Biobank framework (“across 813 traits”), which domain knowledge flags as systematically less reliable than disease-focused models when such models exist. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All 6 candidates are direct matches (trait_efo=cervical carcinoma; phenotyping_reported is cervical cancer/incident cervical cancer). PGS003428 is best supported overall because it comes from a cervical-phenotype-focused GWAS meta-analysis study (publication explicitly about cervical phenotypes and risk stratification), uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred) with very large variant count (2,894,555), and reports a moderate per-SD effect size (HR=1.33). The main limitation is that only full-model discrimination is reported (C-index=0.613) with no explicit PRS-only AUROC/R2, and its training sample size is relatively small (n=4,295), so the evidence does not clearly dominate all alternatives.

Runner-up PGS000073 is supported by a large European evaluation (n=211,795) with incident cervical cancer endpoint and similar covariates, plus reported HR=1.22 and C-index=0.75; however, it is a GWAS-hits score with only 10 variants and the reported AUROC/C-index appear to be full-model metrics (domain guidance: do not infer PRS quality from full-model AUROC alone). Runner-up PGS005165 is the best-supported non-EUR option with an East Asian GWAS/EVAL context (EAS 100%), incident cervical cancer endpoint, and HR=1.2, but its discrimination evidence is modest (C-index=0.566) and it is also a small GWAS-hits model (15 variants), limiting standalone PRS strength inference.

All 6 candidates are direct matches to cholelithiasis (either exact cholelithiasis/K80 or a closely related composite including cholecystitis). PGS001174 is preferred because it is the only candidate with explicit PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.623 and PGS-only R² 0.028) plus incremental/full-model AUROC reported under basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), and its PGS-only R² is plausibly below the provided EUR heritability ceiling (h2_obs=0.0214; noting scale differences, it does not appear grossly inconsistent). Main limitation: it comes from a pan-trait UKB framework paper and uses a time-to-event phenotype, both of which the domain guidance flags as potential generalization weaknesses versus disease-focused scores; however, the competing candidates largely lack PRS-only AUC/R², making them harder to justify as clearly superior from the visible evidence.

Runners-up: PGS002072 and PGS001861 share the same endpoint (cholelithiasis and cholecystitis), same publication family, and provide partial-correlation estimates with CIs (0.098 and 0.0948, respectively), offering some quantitative support despite lacking PRS-only AUROC/R². Between them, PGS002072 is ranked above PGS001861 due to slightly higher partial-r and use of a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2) versus penalized regression, with otherwise similar metadata. Other direct-match candidates (PGS004476/PGS004546) report only per-SD ORs (~1.22 and ~1.30) with unknown covariates and no PRS-comparable discrimination metrics, and PGS005150 is evaluated only in East Asian ancestry (EAS-only evaluation), limiting general direct-match support when deployment ancestry is unspecified.

All listed candidates are direct matches at the EFO level (chronic kidney disease), but they vary in endpoint fidelity and how interpretable the reported performance is as PRS signal. PGS002237 is best supported because it is explicitly CKD-focused (Nat Med: “Genome-wide polygenic score to predict chronic kidney disease across ancestries”), uses a clear clinically meaningful endpoint (CKD stage 3+; eGFR <45), has multi-ancestry evaluation, and reports a strong full-model AUROC (0.78) plus a moderate per-SD effect size (OR 1.47). Although its AUROC is full-model and covariate-heavy (many clinical covariates), the combination of disease-focused design + endpoint specificity + effect size support makes it the most defensible direct-match pick from the visible evidence.

Runner-up 1 (PGS005090) is also CKD stage 3+ and reports very strong discrimination (AUROC 0.9; R² 0.1; OR 1.41) in an African American/Afro-Caribbean evaluation, making it highly compelling for that ancestry context; however, the evidence is limited to a single ancestry evaluation and the very high full-model metrics are not accompanied by PRS-only metrics, so comparability/generalizability across settings is less clear.

Runner-up 2 (PGS004158) is the top performer within a coherent cluster of same-endpoint CKD models from the same publication family (“Evaluation of polygenic scoring methods in five biobanks…”) with covariates listed as 0 (clean comparability) and the highest full-model AUROC among its siblings (~0.592). Its limitation is that this family’s reported AUROCs are modest and still full-model (not explicitly PRS-only), and the development sample size is relatively small (n=13,496), so it is less strongly supported than the Nat Med CKD-focused score.

Other direct-match candidates were deprioritized due to weaker/less coherent phenotype alignment (e.g., PGS000728 uses eGFR rather than CKD diagnosis; PGS001272 is a pan-trait UKB framework sparse score with low PGS-only AUROC ~0.536 and low PGS-only R² ~0.002; PGS000859 appears phenotype-misaligned to diabetes subtype; PGS004224 is packaged around secondhand smoke exposure; PGS004889 is incident CKD without diabetes with a clinical risk-score covariate bundle; several others lack PRS-comparable metrics and/or have less disease-focused context).

All 10 candidates are direct matches via trait_efo mapping to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, but they vary in endpoint fidelity and study archetype. PGS001783 is preferred because it is an exact COPD endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both COPD) and comes from a large multi-biobank/global analysis using a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto), with PRS-comparable performance evidence (Nagelkerke R2 with covariates regressed out = 0.038092) that is consistent with the provided COPD heritability ceiling guidance (h2_liability=0.0388). The main limitation is that its AUROC is only reported as a generic AUROC (0.74) without an explicit PGS-only AUROC, and the validation sample size shown for this model is relatively small (n=7,128), lowering certainty.

Runner-up PGS001788 is from the same publication and method family with the same COPD endpoint and much larger validation sample size (n=337,168), but it has weaker PRS-comparable R2 (0.0163), so it ranks behind PGS001783 on comparable PRS signal strength. The second runner-up PGS001332 is an exact COPD endpoint with explicit PGS-only AUROC/R2 reported (PGS-only AUROC 0.53971; PGS-only R2 0.00235) and clean/basic covariates, but it is from a pan-trait sparse UK Biobank framework ("across 813 traits" snpnet) which domain guidance flags as tending to generalize poorly; its PRS-only metrics are also notably weaker than the PRS-comparable R2 reported for PGS001783/PGS001788. Overall, direct-match candidates exist, but mixed metric comparability (PGS-only vs covariates-regressed-out R2 vs effect-size-only) and framework-vs-multi-biobank differences prevent a clearly unambiguous high-confidence pick.

All 6 candidates are direct matches to the target concept (cirrhosis of liver), but they vary in endpoint specificity (generic cirrhosis vs alcohol-related subtypes) and in how PRS-relevant performance is reported (mostly full-model metrics or effect sizes rather than PRS-only AUC/R²). All four candidates are direct-match to the target disease family (juvenile idiopathic arthritis), come from the same disease-focused publication (Ann Rheum Dis; "Genomic risk scores for juvenile idiopathic arthritis and its subtypes."), use the same method (SparSNP), and have similar basic covariates (sex, genetic PCs 1–10) with EUR-only development/evaluation—so phenotype alignment is the primary differentiator. PGS000114 is the only model whose trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported are the broad umbrella endpoint "Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis" rather than a specific subtype, making it the best-supported direct match for a generic JIA target. The runners-up are subtype models with strong internal support but narrower endpoint fidelity: PGS000325 (oligoarticular JIA) is ranked ahead of PGS000326 (RF-negative polyarticular JIA) due to stronger reported discrimination/effect size in the selected European validation record (full-model AUROC 0.80; OR 1.93 vs AUROC 0.76; OR 1.51). Confidence is Moderate because the available performance metrics are full-model AUROC (not explicitly PRS-only), and the highest-AUROC subtype model (PGS000324; AUROC 0.93) is not selected as primary due to being a narrower subtype endpoint despite strong reported performance.

All 10 listed candidates are direct matches to the target trait (kidney cancer) via trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (kidney cancer / renal carcinoma / renal cell carcinoma; several explicitly incident kidney cancer). PGS004908 is best supported in the visible evidence because it has strong endpoint alignment (phenotyping_reported: Kidney cancer), the strongest reported discrimination among candidates (AUROC 0.74 with CI 0.72–0.75 in European validation), and a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.5, CI 1.43–1.58), with covariates that are standard epidemiologic/demographic (age, sex, PCs, BMI, smoking, hypertension) rather than obvious clinical leakage. The two strongest runners-up are PGS000076 and PGS000787: both are tightly endpoint-aligned (incident kidney cancer; renal cell carcinoma is the clinically dominant subtype of kidney cancer per provided domain knowledge), have large European validation (n=391,610), and report similar full-model AUROC (~0.722) plus HR per SD ~1.15–1.16. Confidence is Moderate (not High) because most candidates lack PRS-only (covariate-free) performance metrics, several reported AUROCs are full-model and thus not directly comparable across differing covariate sets, and PGS000787 is described as an inverse-weight variant of PGS000076 (raising ambiguity about standalone PRS construction despite similar metrics).

Direct-match candidates for the target trait (kidney failure) are present, including PGS004562 (N18 chronic renal failure; trait_efo=kidney failure), PGS004492 (N18 chronic renal failure; trait_efo=kidney failure), and PGS000708 (Kidney failure; trait_efo=kidney failure). PGS004562 is best supported within this list because it is endpoint-aligned (explicit chronic renal failure/kidney failure) and shows the strongest reported per-SD effect size among the kidney-failure-labeled options (OR=1.39548 vs OR=1.1708 for PGS004492 and HR=1.19 for PGS000708). Main limitation: for PGS004562 (and PGS004492) covariates are listed as Unknown and there are no PRS-comparable discrimination metrics (no PGS-only AUC/R²), lowering certainty; additionally, PGS000708’s phenotype is explicitly restricted to diabetic kidney failure, which is a narrower endpoint than generic kidney failure despite having a reported C-index (0.779) that may be covariate-influenced. Given these evidence gaps and endpoint heterogeneity across the direct-match set, the overall direct-match recommendation is sub-optimal rather than clearly high-quality.

All 7 candidates are direct matches to the target concept via trait_efo=osteoarthritis, knee (or a closely related knee-OA endpoint). The best-supported choice is PGS002767 because it has strong endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported: knee osteoarthritis), uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS; 1,052,275 variants), and reports a comparatively strong PRS effect size (OR=1.35 per SD, EUR eval), which is meaningful PRS-specific evidence even without AUC/R2. Runner-up PGS002729 is also tightly aligned (clinical osteoarthritis; knee osteoarthritis) and disease-focused, but its only visible discrimination metric is a full-model AUROC=0.66 with covariates including BMI and no PGS-only metrics, making PRS-only comparability weaker. Runner-up PGS001192 has explicit PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.5566; PGS-only R2=0.0068) and multi-ancestry evaluation, but it comes from a known pan-trait sparse UKB framework paper (snpnet; 4,525 variants) and uses a time-to-event endpoint, both of which are negative/limiting signals for external generalization relative to disease-focused knee-OA scores. Overall confidence is moderate because most candidates lack PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUC/R2), and several are near-indistinguishable on endpoint alignment with incomplete covariate/performance reporting.

All 5 candidates are direct matches by trait_reported/trait_efo to late-onset Alzheimer’s disease, but the pool lacks clearly PRS-comparable metrics (no PGS-only AUROC/R² reported). Selection therefore relies mainly on endpoint fidelity plus available effect-size evidence and structural signals.

PGS000054 is preferred because it is endpoint-faithful (familial late-onset AD/LOAD), uses basic covariates (age, sex), and provides the strongest available PRS-discrimination proxy in the set: OR per SD = 1.73 (95% CI 1.57–1.93) in an explicit evaluation ancestry (AMR/Hispanic/Latin American). This OR≥1.5 is strong supportive evidence per the provided domain guidance.

Runners-up: PGS000053 is the closest sibling (same publication, same 21-variant GWAS-significant approach, same phenotype framing and covariates) but shows a weaker OR per SD (1.29), making it less supported on the only directly comparable performance signal. PGS000334 remains a plausible alternative due to direct LO-AD endpoint and a reported R²=0.191, but that R² is a full-model/unspecified metric from a C+T pipeline with unknown covariates and is flagged by the domain guidance as potentially non-comparable/suspect at this magnitude, so it is ranked behind the effect-size-supported Neurology siblings.

Main limitation: absence of PRS-only AUROC/R² across the candidate set and several ‘Unknown’ covariate fields (notably PGS000334/PGS002289/PGS004918) prevent a high-confidence, clearly best-supported choice.

Direct-match candidates for lung cancer are present (multiple models with trait_reported/phenotyping_reported aligned to lung cancer or closely overlapping lung/bronchus cancer). PGS000078 is best supported in the visible list because it has strong endpoint alignment (phenotyping_reported: incident lung cancer; trait_efo: lung carcinoma), very large validation sample size (n=392,539), and includes effect-size evidence (HR 1.16, 95% CI 1.11–1.22) alongside reported discrimination (full-model AUROC 0.846; C-index 0.849). However, confidence is not high because the reported AUROC/C-index are full-model metrics with extensive covariates (including family history, PM2.5, and detailed smoking interaction terms), and no PRS-only AUROC/R2 is provided, making cross-model PRS comparability limited. Runner-up PGS000789 is essentially the same lung-cancer PRS (explicitly derived from PGS000078’s 109 variants) with the same large validation size and similar metrics (AUROC 0.846; HR 1.17), but it is not clearly stronger than the original and uses the same covariate-heavy evaluation context. Second runner-up PGS004860 has strong reported discrimination (full-model AUROC 0.893; R² 0.49) and clear endpoint alignment (incident lung cancer), but it is supported by a much smaller validation sample (n=24,012) and still lacks PRS-only metrics; its very high full-model performance could be partly covariate-driven, limiting direct PRS comparability. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All listed candidates are direct matches to the target trait (lupus erythematosus) via either the exact EFO term (lupus erythematosus) or the closely aligned clinical entity systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). For a generic lupus erythematosus target, models with phenotype-aligned SLE diagnosis endpoints are acceptable direct matches, while restricted/sub-phenotypes (e.g., lupus nephritis-only, renal disease age-of-onset, early-onset-only, or broad ‘erythematous conditions’) are less endpoint-faithful.

Best pick: PGS000754 is preferred because it targets SLE with a straightforward phenotype (“Systemic lupus erythematosus”) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (lassosum) with very large variant count (293,684), which is a positive structural signal for polygenic prediction compared with GWAS-hit-only scores. Its reported metric is only a full-model AUROC (0.65) and not PRS-only, so performance comparability is limited; nonetheless, among the endpoint-faithful options it has the strongest method/coverage evidence.

Runners-up: (1) PGS000328 has a reasonably aligned endpoint but is explicitly restricted to early-onset SLE (“onset before age 20”), which is a meaningful endpoint restriction for a generic lupus target; it does report a higher full-model AUROC (0.83) but this is not PRS-only and thus discounted. (2) PGS004917 matches SLE diagnosis and reports both AUROC (0.696) and a strong effect size (OR 2.01), which is supportive, but it is a GWAS-hit clumped score (97 variants) and comes from an interaction-focused context (“…and Smoking”), with covariates unspecified—both limit interpretability versus a genome-wide shrinkage disease-risk score.

Main limitation driving DIRECT_SUB_OPTIMAL: across the pool, the available performance evidence is largely non-PRS-comparable (mostly full-model AUROC with unknown covariates), and several candidates have endpoint restrictions or potential leakage/packaging concerns (e.g., PGS003960 uses a ‘phenotype risk score’ covariate; PGS000196 is in an arthritis outpatient diagnostic-prioritization setting; PGS000803 has mismatched phenotyping_reported). This prevents a clearly high-confidence single winner despite a reasonable structural preference for PGS000754.

Direct-match candidates for the target concept (lymphoid/lymphocytic leukemia) are present (e.g., PGS000788, PGS000077, PGS000645; others are chronic lymphocytic leukemia subtypes). PGS000788 is best supported within the visible evidence because its phenotyping_reported is an incident lymphocytic leukemia endpoint aligned to the target, it reports a comparatively strong per-SD effect size (HR=1.7) and the highest reported full-model discrimination among the direct lymphoid/lymphocytic-leukemia-labeled models (AUROC=0.738; C-index=0.756) with only basic covariates (age/sex/array/PCs). However, confidence is not high because the reported AUROC/C-index are full-model metrics (no PGS-only AUROC/R2), and PGS000788’s method is explicitly derived from PGS000077 with inverse weights, creating ambiguity about whether the apparent performance difference reflects PRS quality versus modeling/packaging differences. Runner-up PGS000077 has the same incident lymphocytic leukemia endpoint and identical covariate set with a slightly weaker effect size (HR=1.45) and lower full-model AUROC (0.719), but it is the original genome-wide-significant-variant score rather than an inverse-weight derivative. The second runner-up PGS000645 is a direct lymphoid leukemia label/endpoint but has much weaker reported discrimination (AUROC=0.578) and a very small variant set (6), limiting support despite being a clean direct match.

All 7 candidates are direct matches to the target concept (macular degeneration / age-related macular degeneration), but the evidence is uneven and sometimes non-comparable (several lack PRS-only AUC/R²; one has an apparent AUROC formatting issue). PGS004606 is best supported because it has strong endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported: Age-related macular degeneration; trait_efo: age-related macular degeneration), comes from a disease-focused AMD GWAS study (Nat Genet 2024), uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS; ~1,000,946 variants), and reports a full-model AUROC of 0.71 with only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), plus a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.76, 95% CI 1.73–1.78), which is supportive of meaningful PRS signal. Main limitation: it does not report PRS-only discrimination (PGS-only AUROC/R² are null), so the AUROC is not directly comparable across models and confidence cannot be high.

Runners-up: (1) PGS004607 is from the same disease-focused Nat Genet 2024 study with the same clean AMD endpoint and covariates and similar genome-wide PRS-CS construction (~1,067,520 variants), but has weaker reported performance/effect size (full-model AUROC 0.65; OR 1.48) and a GWAS ancestry listed as AFR with EUR evaluation, making it less straightforwardly supported than PGS004606 for a generic (unspecified-ancestry) target. (2) PGS001013 is an exact-label ‘Macular degeneration’ model with explicit PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.55283; PGS-only R² 0.00599) and incremental AUROC reported, but it is from a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse framework paper (‘across 813 traits’), which domain guidance flags as typically underperforming disease-focused scores in external validation; its PRS-only metrics are also modest. PGS004952 is not ranked in the top 3 despite a very high reported AUROC because only full-model AUROC is shown and the AUROC value appears inconsistent (classification_metrics shows 84.2 rather than 0.842), and validation n is small (1,232), making the performance evidence ambiguous in this context.

Direct-match melanoma PRS candidates are present (multiple models with trait_efo=melanoma / phenotyping_reported melanoma or incident invasive melanoma). Among the visible candidates, PGS002247 is best supported because it has strong endpoint fidelity (incident invasive melanoma), is disease-focused (independent evaluation of melanoma PRS in prospective cohorts), and reports comparatively strong discrimination evidence (full_model_auc=0.691 with R²=0.072) in European validation. The two strongest runners-up from the same list are PGS002246 (same publication family, same endpoint, very similar performance: full_model_auc=0.688; R²=0.07) and PGS000743 (melanoma endpoint with notably higher reported full_model_auc=0.74, but with much smaller validation sample size n=1,035 and no PRS-only metrics, making its apparent advantage less secure). Overall confidence is Moderate because most candidates report only full-model AUROC (often with differing covariate sets), PRS-only metrics are generally absent, and several near-tied direct-match models exist, limiting a clearly dominant choice.

All six candidates are nominally direct-match on trait_reported/trait_efo (multiple myeloma / plasma cell myeloma), but endpoint fidelity differs: PGS000652/PGS000653/PGS000654 and PGS002281/PGS002306 all report phenotyping_reported = Multiple myeloma, whereas PGS003450 has an explicit mismatch (phenotyping_reported = Chronic lymphocytic leukemia) and is therefore weak for direct-match despite the trait label.

Among the endpoint-faithful set, PGS002281 has the strongest visible discrimination evidence (full-model AUROC 0.644 with CI 0.622–0.666) plus a strong stratification metric (OR highest vs lowest quintiles 3.18, CI 2.34–4.33) in a reasonably sized European evaluation (n=2,395) with basic covariates (age, sex, geographic region). However, the evidence remains limited for a “high-quality” designation because none of the candidates report PRS-only AUROC/R² (domain guidance: do not treat full-model AUROC as PRS-comparable), and PGS002281 lists samples_training as N/A with no training/development cohorts shown.

Runners-up: PGS000653 and PGS000654 are endpoint-faithful siblings from the same publication family with similar covariates (age/sex/PCs/batch) and larger validation (n=2,738). They also report per-SD effect sizes (OR ~1.33 and ~1.32, respectively) and slightly higher full-model AUROC than PGS000652, making them the best-supported alternatives within that coherent cluster. PGS002306 shows a higher full-model AUROC (0.69) but on a much smaller validation sample (n=290) and with unknown covariates, reducing comparability and confidence versus the better-documented alternatives.

All 7 visible candidates are direct matches to the target trait (multiple sclerosis) by trait_efo and phenotyping_reported, so a direct-match selection is possible. PGS000809 is preferred because it comes from a disease-focused MS study context (multi-cohort MS genetics consortia-style development listed) with a direct MS endpoint and reports discrimination (full-model AUROC 0.765 with basic covariates age/sex/PCs), avoiding the known framework/portability penalties that apply to the UKB pan-trait sparse snpnet models (PGS001270/PGS001271) and the UKB portability paper models (PGS001831/PGS002038). The main limitation is that across the pool, PRS-comparable metrics are sparse: PGS000809 reports only full-model AUROC/R² (not PGS-only), and several competitors either lack AUROC entirely (partial-r only) or report full-model AUROC with unknown covariates (PGS002726), making cross-model performance comparisons uncertain; therefore confidence is not high. Runner-up PGS002726 is supported by the highest reported full-model AUROC (0.80) and a strong OR (top 10% vs median 15.0), but its covariates are unknown and validation n is small (n=938), reducing comparability. Runner-up PGS002038 is methodologically strong (LDpred2 genome-wide shrinkage; very large variant count) but provides only partial correlation (partial-r 0.0396) without AUROC/R², and it comes from a portability framework publication, so its direct-match support is weaker than disease-focused MS-specific candidates despite clean endpoint labeling.

Direct-match candidates for myocardial infarction are present (multiple models with trait_efo/phenotyping_reported indicating myocardial infarction or acute myocardial infarction). Among the visible MI-specific set, PGS005039 (Myocardial infarction, PheCode 411.2) has the strongest reported discrimination in the provided metadata (C-index 0.784836989151752) and a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.578, 95% CI 1.50–1.67), with a disease-diagnosis endpoint (phenotyping_reported: Myocardial infarction) and basic covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs). Runners-up: PGS005040 (same endpoint; C-index 0.76866638941772 but weaker OR 1.071) is supported by comparable endpoint fidelity but less PRS signal; PGS005035 (same endpoint; C-index 0.783355229253263; OR 1.541, 95% CI 1.46–1.63) is very close to the best and remains a strong alternative. Limitation: across these candidates, the reported discrimination is a full-model C-index (not explicitly PRS-only), and several near-tied MI models exist (including UKB pan-trait snpnet MI variants and acute MI ICD10 I21 models with limited comparable metrics), so the choice is not uniquely decisive from the visible evidence alone.

Both visible candidates are direct matches to the target trait (trait_efo = Nasal Cavity Polyp; phenotyping_reported = ICD10 J33 Nasal polyp) and come from the same publication, with identical training cohort (UKB), training size (n=174,489), validation size (n=56,192), and EUR-only development/evaluation—so endpoint fidelity and transportability are essentially tied. Neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, leaving effect size as the main differentiator; PGS004535 shows a stronger per-SD odds ratio (OR=1.600668, meeting the domain-knowledge ‘strong’ OR≥1.5 guideline) versus PGS004465 (OR=1.3496, ‘moderate’), so PGS004535 is best supported on the available evidence. Overall outcome is still DIRECT_SUB_OPTIMAL because key comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUC/R2) and covariate details are missing for both, limiting confidence and making within-family method differences (RFDiseasemetaPRS vs LDpred2) hard to interpret beyond the observed OR.

Two direct-match candidates are present (both map to nicotine dependence via trait_efo and report the same endpoint label in phenotyping_reported: Tobacco use disorder) from the same publication family and with similar basic covariates, so endpoint fidelity is essentially tied. The main differentiator in the visible evidence is PRS-comparable performance: PGS002037 shows higher partial correlation in the selected European validation record (partial-r 0.0741, CI 0.0601–0.0881) than PGS001830 (partial-r 0.0557, CI 0.0416–0.0697), supporting PGS002037 as best. Structural signals also mildly favor PGS002037 (LDpred2 genome-wide shrinkage; 847,691 variants) over PGS001830 (penalized regression; 13,838 variants), consistent with stronger polygenic signal capture. Confidence is Moderate because both models come from a UKB portability framework paper (not disease-focused), and neither provides AUC/R2 or PRS-only AUROC/R2—leaving partial-r as the only comparable metric.

All 7 candidates are direct matches to the target concept (nodular goiter) via either benign nodular goiter or nontoxic multinodular goiter endpoints. The strongest direct-match support comes from the coherent disease-focused multi-cohort thyroid/benign thyroid disease study family (PGS005261/PGS005262/PGS005263), which provides explicit case-control discrimination (full-model AUROC) and per-SD effect sizes; within this family, PGS005262 is best supported because it has the highest reported AUROC (0.5933) and the strongest reported effect size (OR 1.408 per SD) among the benign nodular goiter scores, with the same endpoint label and evaluation context as its siblings. Runners-up are PGS005263 (same endpoint/method family with slightly weaker AUROC/OR) and then PGS005261 (same endpoint but structurally weaker P+T method and much smaller variant count, despite similar AUROC). The main limitation is that the AUROC values shown for the 2026 models are full-model metrics with unknown covariates (so they are not clean PRS-only comparators), and the alternative UKB portability scores (PGS001814/PGS002022) report only small partial correlations without AUC/OR, making cross-family comparison uncertain; therefore confidence is moderate and the overall outcome is direct-match but sub-optimal rather than clearly high-quality.

All 10 candidates are direct matches to the target trait (obesity) via trait_efo and/or phenotyping_reported. The best-supported choice is PGS002033 because it has strong phenotype alignment ("Overweight, obesity and other hyperalimentation"), uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2) with very large variant count (846,292), and reports a PRS-comparable metric (partial correlation 0.0789 with CI) in European validation; within the same publication family, it also has stronger reported partial-r than its penalized-regression sibling PGS001825 (0.0547). Runners-up: (1) PGS001825 is the closest sibling with the same endpoint and study context but weaker partial-r and far fewer variants (13,009). (2) PGS005235 is endpoint-faithful (phenotyping_reported: "Obesity (phecode: 278.1)") and has a strong per-SD effect size signal (OR 1.97) with a large-variant LDpred2-auto construction, but lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R2 and comes from a different study context, making it harder to compare directly. Overall confidence is moderate because most candidates lack directly comparable PRS-only AUC/R2, and some alternatives have strong effect sizes but incomplete/heterogeneous performance reporting, limiting a clearly definitive ranking. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All 13 candidates are direct matches to the target trait (osteoporosis) by trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported, but most lack PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC/R²) or report only modest effect sizes, making the overall direct-match choice evidence-limited.

Best pick: PGS005155 is a direct osteoporosis model with phenotype-aligned endpoint (“Osteoporosis”), evaluated in an East Asian cohort (EVAL: EAS 100%, n=58,611) and built with PRS-CSx using mixed EUR+EAS GWAS (EAS 28%, EUR 72%). Among the candidates that report only effect sizes (no AUC/R²), it has the strongest reported effect size (β=1.1443) and a clear cross-ancestry construction (PRS-CSx) that is structurally favorable versus single-ancestry PRS-CS in the same study context.

Runners-up: (1) PGS005146 is the closest sibling comparator (same endpoint, same evaluation cohort/ancestry and sample size, same method family PRS-CS) but with a weaker reported effect size (β=1.0937) and no cross-ancestry extension. (2) PGS004810 is also endpoint-aligned (“Osteoporosis”), uses an ensemble-style method (PRSmixPlus; structurally favorable per domain guidance), and reports an incremental R² (0.022, EUR eval), but it has a much smaller validation sample (n=9,462) and lacks PRS-only AUROC/R², limiting comparability.

Main limitation driving DIRECT_SUB_OPTIMAL: the pool is dominated by framework/portability-style scores (e.g., UKB ‘813 traits’ snpnet; ‘Portability of 245 polygenic scores’) and several newer models with missing PRS-only discrimination metrics; where full-model AUROC is shown (e.g., PGS001273/PGS001274), incremental AUROC and PGS-only R² are small, suggesting covariate-driven performance and reducing confidence in using those AUROCs for PRS ranking.

Both visible candidates are direct matches to otosclerosis (trait_efo=otosclerosis). PGS002046 is preferred because its endpoint is a generic otosclerosis phenotype (phenotyping_reported="Otosclerosis"), avoiding the time-to-event formulation that domain guidance flags as a potential endpoint-fidelity warning for generic disease-risk use. It also uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2) with substantially broader variant coverage (570,308 variants), which is a supportive structural signal versus the very sparse snpnet model (213 variants) from a pan-trait UKB framework paper. Main limitation: PGS002046 lacks PRS-comparable AUROC/R² in the provided metrics (only partial-r is reported), so the choice relies heavily on endpoint/method/structure rather than directly comparable discrimination metrics. Runner-up PGS001255 remains a direct match and provides explicit PGS-only AUROC/R² and incremental AUROC, but is penalized by time-to-event phenotyping and its pan-trait sparse-framework provenance with very low variant count. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

Direct-match candidates are present (multiple ovarian cancer / ovarian carcinoma / ovarian neoplasm models). PGS000082 is best supported overall because it targets incident ovarian cancer (phenotyping_reported), is evaluated in Europeans, and has the strongest visible discrimination among broadly aligned, non-restricted endpoints in this list (full-model AUROC ~0.656 / C-index ~0.655) with very large validation (n=211,958). Key limitation: the reported AUROC/C-index are full-model metrics with substantial covariate adjustment (including family history and multiple epidemiologic factors), and no PRS-only AUC/R² is provided, so PRS-only performance is uncertain; this keeps confidence below High. Runner-up PGS000793 is closely related (same 36-variant basis from PGS000082) with similar endpoint/covariates and slightly higher full-model AUROC (~0.66), but it is a derivative/inverse-weight variant and does not clearly improve PRS-only evidence. Second runner-up PGS003385 shows the highest AUROC in the list (~0.717) but is for the serous carcinoma subtype (not the full ovarian neoplasm umbrella) and still lacks PRS-only metrics; subtype restriction reduces direct-match breadth despite strong reported discrimination. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All 11 listed candidates are direct matches to the target trait (pancreatic carcinoma) via pancreatic cancer endpoints (mostly EFO: exocrine pancreatic carcinoma) or the clinically dominant subtype pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PGS002264). Best-supported pick is PGS000083 because it has strong endpoint fidelity (incident pancreatic cancer), large European evaluation (n=391,491), and supportive effect-size evidence (HR 1.49, 95% CI 1.36–1.62) with consistent discrimination reported (AUROC 0.745; C-index 0.742). Main limitation: the reported AUROC/C-index are full-model metrics with multiple covariates (including family history and smoking/BMI), and no PRS-only AUROC/R² is provided, so standalone PRS performance is uncertain.

Runners-up: (1) PGS000794 is essentially the same 22-variant score family (explicitly derived from PGS000083, with very similar endpoint/covariates and identical AUROC 0.745 and HR 1.49), but its construction note (“inverse variant weights”) introduces ambiguity without clear evidence of superiority over the original. (2) PGS000663 remains endpoint-faithful (pancreatic cancer, 0–10 years follow-up) and shows a comparable per-SD effect size (OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.25–1.67) with some cross-ancestry evaluation (EAS/EUR), but it has much smaller validation (n=956) and includes biomarker/risk-factor integration context, making its reported full-model AUROC (0.67) less directly comparable for PRS ranking. PGS002264 reports a very high AUROC (0.83) but is heavily clinically packaged (diabetes status/onset, waist circumference, family history), so that full-model AUROC is discounted for standalone PRS selection despite subtype alignment.

All 11 candidates are direct matches at the disease-concept level (trait_efo=Parkinson disease), but several are progression/dementia endpoints (PGS000056, PGS000211, PGS000777) rather than generic PD risk/status, which weakens them for the target trait. Among the generic PD endpoints, PGS000903 (Lancet Neurol 2021 meta-analysis) has strong endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported: Parkinson's disease), a disease-focused multi-cohort development context, and the richest PRS signal capture (C+T with 1,805 variants) plus the strongest PRS-relevant association evidence shown (OR top vs bottom quartile 6.25; reported R²=0.054, though it is not explicitly labeled PRS-only). PGS000902 is a close sibling from the same publication family with the same endpoint and covariates but uses only genome-wide significant variants (90 SNPs) and shows lower full-model AUROC (0.651 vs 0.692), making it a plausible runner-up. PGS003763 is also endpoint-faithful (incident PD) with a large evaluation sample and a clear HR separation (1.72 high vs low tertile), but it lacks comparable PRS-only metrics and is incident-only, so it ranks behind the Lancet Neurol meta-analysis scores. Confidence is moderate (not high) because most reported AUROCs appear to be full-model (covariate-influenced) rather than explicitly PRS-only, and covariate sets differ across candidates (some include family history or broader risk-factor bundles), limiting clean cross-model comparability.

All four candidates are direct matches in the broad sense of peripheral vascular disease, but they split into (i) two UKB portability-framework scores for “Peripheral vascular disease, unspecified” (PGS001843, PGS002055) and (ii) two disease-focused “Peripheral artery disease” scores (PGS005158, PGS005217). Given domain guidance prioritizing endpoint fidelity and disease-focused study archetype over portability-framework scores, PGS005217 is best supported: it targets incident peripheral artery disease (a core component of peripheral vascular disease), comes from a PAD-focused multi-cohort study (many contributing cohorts listed), uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2) with large variant count (1,296,292), and reports a strong PRS effect size (HR 1.66 per SD) plus a full-model C-index (0.731) with relatively basic covariates (age, sex, PCs). Main limitation: the target is broader (“peripheral vascular disease”) than PAD, and the reported discrimination is full-model (not explicitly PGS-only), so standalone PRS performance comparability remains uncertain.

Runners-up: Among the remaining models, PGS002055 is preferred over PGS001843 because both are from the same UKB portability framework with the same “PVD unspecified” phenotype and similar covariates, but PGS002055 shows slightly higher partial correlation (0.0175 vs 0.0151) and is structurally stronger (LDpred2 with 599,514 variants vs penalized regression with 242 variants). PGS001843 is the next best-supported as the other exact-label PVD candidate, but its very low variant count and weaker partial-r reduce support.
